chunk_text: And given the incredible amount of progress in AI We wanted to pick something really ambitious Something that we thought you couldn't just Tackle by scaling up existing approaches That you really needed something new in order to address And we landed on Diplomacy because we Thought that it would be the hardest game to make an AI for What is Diplomacy Diplomacy is a natural language strategy game It takes place right before World War I You play as one of the seven great powers of Europe England, France, Germany, Austria, Russia, and Turkey And your goal is to control the majority of the map In practice that rarely happens, if you Control a majority of the map then you've Won, in practice, nobody ends up winning outright And so your score is proportional to the percentage Of the map that you control Now, what's really interesting about Diplomacy Is that it is a natural language negotiation game You have these conversations, what you're seeing here Between Germany and England where they will privately

chunk_text: Communicate with each other before making their moves And so you can have Germany ask, want to support Sweden England says, let me think on that, and so on This is a popular strategy game developed in the 1950s It was JFK and Kissinger's favorite game And I said, each turn involves Sophisticated private natural language negotiations And I want to make clear, this is not negotiations You would see in a game Settlers of Catan For example You're seeing it's much more Survivor If you've ever seen the TV show Survivor You have discussions around alliances That you'd to build, discussions Around specific tactics that you'd To execute on the current turn, and also more longt Strategy around where do we go from here And how do we divide resources Now, the way the game works, you have these negotiations That lasts between 5 and 15 minutes, depending On the version of the game on each turn And all these negotiations are done privately Pairwise negotiation Also, that you are not muted

chunk_text: Cicero is an AI agent for Diplomacy That integrates high level strategic play and open domain Dialogue And we use 50,000 human games of Diplomacy Acquired through a partnership with the website Webdiplomacy.net We entered Cicero in an online diplomacy league Just to give you the results up front Cicero was not detected as an AI agent For 40 games with 82 unique players There was one player that mentioned after the fact that They made a joke about us being a bot But they didn't really follow up on it And nobody else followed up on it And they later accused somebody else of also being a bot We weren't sure how seriously to take that accusation But it's safe to say it made it through all 40 games Without being detected as bot And then in fact, when we told the players afterwards That it was a bot the whole time These are the kinds of responses that we got People were quite surprised, pleasantly surprised Fortunately Nobody was upset with us

chunk_text: Model That's one main contribution, this Control the dialogue model that conditions on a plan The second is a planning engine that Accounts for dialogue and human behavior I mentioned that a lot of previous work on games Was done using selfplay in twoplayer zerosum settings Now, the problem with pure selfplay Is that it can learn strong policies But it doesn't stick with human conventions And it can't account for dialogue It's just going to ignore the human data and the human way Of playing if you just do selfplay That's one extreme The other extreme that you can go Is to just do supervised learning on human data Create this model of how humans play And then train with those imitation humans And if you do this, you'll end up With a bot that's consistent with dialogue And human conventions But it's only as strong as the training data And we found that it was Very easily manipulable through adversarial dialogue For example, you can send messages to it saying

chunk_text: Hey, everyone Thanks for coming to our CS25 lecture today Today we're honored to have Jim Fan from NVIDIA Who we're talking about generalist Agents in openended worlds And he's a senior AI research scientist At NVIDIA, where his mission is to build generally capable AI Agents with applications to gaming robotics and software Automation And his research spans foundation models Multimodal AI, reinforcement learning And openended learning He obtained his PhD degree in computer science From here, at Stanford, advised by Professor FeiFei Li And previously, he did research internships At OpenAI, Google AI, as well as MilaQuebec AI Institute Give it up for Jim Thanks for having me I want to start with a story of two kittens It's a story that gave me a lot of inspiration over my career I want to share this one first Back in 1963, there are two scientists From MIT, Held and Hein They did this ingenious experiment Where they put two newborn kittens in this device And the kittens have not seen the visual world yet

chunk_text: And so the way this whole data mining Thing works is that it focuses on sentence alignment Everyone is probably super familiar with this Because this is how language models are built now It's , you take common crawl or any other opensource dump Of the web I don't know RedPajama, or whatev You want, CCNet, whatever you want to use these days And you take all of the data You extract all of the text A lot of HTML parsing, and so on, goes into it And the idea is that we want to try to find matching text that Could be a translation We shatter it all into sentences We embed them with different sentence encoder models And then we do a match to try to understand In a multilingual space if the sentences match And so one of the biggest challenges to this Is that the quality of the sentence encoding Is very important If your sentence encoding is not very accurate Then it's impossible to match in this dimensional space

chunk_text: The idea of the meaning being the same And so one of the big things we try to do here in this project Was try to improve the quality of the sentence encoders And so one of the big things that we did Was train sentence encoders with masked language modeling You see that on the left But we also use multilingual distillation Which you see on the right And so previous approaches to sentence encoders And the trend in the research community for a while Was to really try to embed all languages in the same sentence Encoder model Projects XLMR, for example, are in that direction , is pretty widely used The challenge with this when you're Training a lowresource model is that a lot Of your highresource data just overwhelms Your lowresource data And so you don't end up with a very highquality sentence Encoder for those languages What we ended up doing is we had a multilingual teach Model, and we distilled a bunch of student models

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: It's really important to be aware of that And this is why DeepSeek tried to come up With their own scaling laws that work for their data sets And they also conclude that when you have higher quality Data sets, maybe more compute should be allocated to the model Size and not to the data size These are interesting things to keep in mind When it comes to scaling LLMs We have answered the first question, I hope How much data to train LLMs Let's say now you have your compute budget, a fixed Number of GPUs for a certain amount of days And you also know approximately how much data you want to use The question is that, where do you find this type of data For example, Llama 3 was trained on 15 trillion tokens But where do you get 15 trillion tokens That's a huge number To get this data, the two main sources Where you can get very large volume of data Are the web and then GitHub code

chunk_text: There are some other curated sources that are of high quality But are much smaller, Wikipedia books, archive Or StackExchange You can also get data, a new type That's been very trendy recently Which is synthetic data But let's first start with the sources where You can get very large volumes The first one is web data That's web pages And usually, people to create these data Sets, they start from CommonCrawl Which is a public repository of crawled web pages CommonCrawl crawls pages regularly And they publish dumps every few months But if you start from there, you will Need to do some heavy filtering at a very large scale For example, just the latest dump has over 400 terabytes And they have almost 95 dumps That's not a very easy task, and you Will need to have a lot of resources and a team To be able to do that crawling The other option is to use an existing filtered web Data set where researchers already filtered the CommonCrawl And released them

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: And luckily, we do have data sets That are very large and well filtered One of them is the web data FineWeb, that was recently Released by Hugging Face, and it has 15 trillion tokens of web data It's not just a large data set, but it also Has the best performance among the publicly available data Sets And here, for example, it shows the performance Which is an aggregation over multiple popular benchmarks For NLP HellaSwag, MMLU, and others And it's averages them and compares to other data sets C4, RefinedWeb, SlimPajama, and The Pile That was for web You can get 15 trillion tokens easily And then for code data, we have released the stack data Set, which is the largest data set of open source code This data set comes in two versions Version one consisted of six terabytes of permissive code And how we build this data set is That we first cloned all the public repositories on GitHub This gave us over 130 repositories And 100 terabytes of data

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: But we don't want all of that data because a lot of it Can be configs or extensions that we don't need Or languages that are no longer maintained We did some file extension filtering And we ended up with almost 90 terabytes of data After that, we filtered repositories Based on their licenses so we can have permissive licenses Apache 2 or MIT You can have more restrictive licenses GPL We filtered all the repositories that did not Have a permissive license And after that, we did a deduplication To remove files that are similar We ended up with almost 3 terabytes of deduplicated data The stack comes also with a very cool tool for opt out This tool is a space where you can go You can type your GitHub username And it tells you if you have any of your GitHub repositories In the data set And if that's the case, there's also An option to fill a form and request To be removed from all the future trainings of BigCode

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: We did that for the second one, but also for the stack v2 In the v2 is a much larger and enhanced Data set compared to the v1 This time, instead of cloning GitHub repositories We went through Software Heritage Which is an archive of code They already did the scraping and we just extracted the data From their archive And we ended up, after all the filtering With almost 1 trillion tokens, which Is a lot compared to the v1 where we got around 200 Billion tokens at the end We also added some high quality resources GitHub issues Math and coding data sets, and pull requests These data sets, the stack v1, the stack v2 Can be used to train LLMs on code or to train general LLMs And include code as a subset of the general web data This shows how the stack v2 compares to the v1 And you can see that before filtering, it's Almost 10 times larger and after filtering, it's Four or five times larger

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: I talk about how to get web data, how to get code data And then I also mentioned synthetic data And it's this year and last year that synthetic data became very Important for LLM training And that in the next few years It will become even more important And this was mainly sparked by the five Series of models by Microsoft The first paper was called textbooks are all you need And they generated synthetic textbooks using GPT3.5 and GPT4, and they tried to build a new Pretraining corpus that is synthetic and they were able To match and outperform models that are trained on web data Sets This model was trained on almost entirely synthetic data But now, some of the very popular LLMs Are using synthetic data as part of their pretraining mix For example, Claude 3, in the model car They say that they generate data internally And they include it in the pretraining This is also the case for Llama 3 Where they use the LLMs to build classifiers

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: That would annotate samples and only keep the high quality ones But they also generated synthetic content To improve performance on coding and reasoning and long contexts Synthetic data is a very new topic But it seems really interesting I'm personally working also on that as Hugging Face We recently released a data set called Cosmopedia, which Was the largest data set of synthetic texts And it had almost 25 billion tokens And instead of using closed models GPT4 It used an open source model, which is Mixtral8x7B And we also released a blog post that Explains how we created this data set Because it can be very tricky to get very diverse samples We used an approach where we had 80 of the data that comes from the web And then we try to use these web samples to build New prompts that ask models to generate text books that Are related to these web samples But while giving them more context We can limit the generations For example, we can have a topic that is a mathematics

chunk_text: And then we have web samples that are related to mathematics And each time we give the model a prompt, generate A textbook in the field of mathematics that Is related to this web sample And the more web samples we add, the more diversity we add We also use some curated sources Stanford courses And wikiHow, where we use extracts from these pages To ask the models to generate content that is related to them You can find more details in the Cosmopedia blog post I guess now, we also have the answ For our second question, which was where to find the data And if you're following, we have one question left Which is, how can we filter this data Because for example, if you use CommonCrawl and you need To filter it, and even if you use the stack We did not train our models on the stack directly We did a lot of filtering to get a data set that is small But has a higher quality

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: And for this data set, I will cite this slide From Thomas Wolfe's presentation This lecture is very interesting, by the way You can find it here And this is from the Yi paper, where They state that a high quality data Set might exhibit very advanced capabilities For a standard architecture And this is the focus of many recent papers And we can see that in model releases The sections about data sets are becoming smaller and small Because people are realizing that the data set is The backbone It is the one that is making some models much bett Than others It's really important to spend A lot of time curating these data sets And trying to remove all the outliers and data Sets that can hurt the model during the training

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: This is the pipeline from the Yi paper for filtering Their crawled web data sets First, they do language filtering I guess in Yi's case, they kept English And some Asian languages Then they apply some filtering techniques To remove low quality samples For example, there are some metrics You look for files that have a lot of lines repeated And then you remove them There's also rulebased collection You also can use perplexity filtering Where you compute something loss And remove samples that have a very high one Then after that, they also did a step Which is very important, deduplication Because there are a lot of papers that Study the effect of duplicates on training And they find that skipping duplicates in the training data Can cause models to memorize and they have less space To be creative This hurts the performance of models And it's always advise to remove duplicates Using exact duplication, to remove Files that are exactly identical, but also Near deduplication to remove files that are similar

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: And this uses techniques MinHash deduplication For Yi, after that, they also did more filtering on top Semantic and topic filtering But usually, you can do the classic filtering And duplication and then be more creative for the other filters This was also the case for FineWeb The reason it is better than other data sets is That because they spent a lot of time trying To come up with better filters and also deduplicate the data Sets well Now the question is, OK, we can do the duplication We have methods that are established to do that We can also do language filtering But then if you want to filter the data to remove garbage And lower quality files, how do you come up with good filters You can for sure find some filters in the literature But if you want to really build a data set that Is better than what exists, you need To invest some time trying to find more techniques That work better for your case

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: This can be done with manual inspection, which is always A good idea to look at the data and see what it Looks And you can come up with filters to help you during the training But that is usually not enough because you Might have an intuition for a filtering that works bett For your model But then when you train, , this filtering Doesn't help And for example, for us, when we were developing the StarCod Series of models, we were thinking, OK What are the best ways for us to filter code We use some standard filters, for example To remove auto generated content But we try to come up with a little bit More complex filtering that could help us Looking for files that have a lot of comments Because code that is usually well documented Is probably of a higher quality than another code file that Doesn't have any comments We implemented this filter that Looks for files that have almost no comments And then removes them

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: And we train the model on that and turned out The performance improvement was really negligible It was not as much as we thought We also tried to use another filter, which Is using the stars of a repository As an indicator of quality We tried removing all the files from repository That have less than five stars, and this ended up removing ov 70 of the data sets And then when we trained on it, the model Was the worst model that we trained in all our ablation Experiments, simply because it removed too much data It was not worth using this filtering technique This is why it's very important that when you have a filter You should run what we call an ablation model The ablation is , you take a subset of your data Set after you applied the filtering And you train a small model on it And see how it behaves with and without the filtering And you might be wondering, OK, if I use a small model

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: But does it really extrapolate to larger models That's a good question But generally, from our experience We found that this does extrapolate For most of data ablations When you're doing these ablations You should select a set of high signal benchmarks That could give you some conclusions About the effect of your filter early in the training This can be some of the popular NLP benchmarks for LLMs For example, HellaSwag or MMLU And you should also Sorry, here it's not tran, it's train with different seeds To reduce the noise because sometimes you Can have filtering techniques that don't give you A very big difference But if you train with just one seed, you must draw conclusions But they're just noise If you can and you have the compute It's always better to run the same experiment with two Or three different seeds, and then Maybe do something the averaging That you reduce the noise and you Have more robust conclusions about the effects Of your filtering For example, for the fine web data set

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: The authors run over 200 plus ablations These were 1 billion models trained on, 30 billion tokens And this is how they were able to find filterings that worked Better for their data sets Now let's go back to our StarCoder use case And I will tell you about how we filtered the stack data sets For the version one, if you remember We had 6 terabytes of source code But when we trained StarCoder, we only Used 800 gigabytes of these 6 terabytes A lot of this data was filtered out after our filtering Or curation The same happened for the stack V2, where this time we Started from 32 in 600 programming languages And after the filtering we ended up With only 6.3 terabytes of code And for filtering code, the approach Is a bit similar to just filtering web data But the filtering techniques are a bit different First, we wanted to include a lot of programming languages And we looked at them and we didn't keep all of them

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: We only kept the popular ones and excluded For example, configs and languages that Are no longer maintained, so this was what V1 For StarCoder 2, we included more languages over 600 And then we added some other sources That could be interesting for a code model to learn from Which are GitHub issues, Git commits, and Jupyter Notebooks We also added for the v2, Kaggle, notebooks, and pull Requests Our second step after we selected The languages we wanted to train on was data quality inspection , as I told you, we had Some filters to remove low quality files And autogenerated content An example is the average line length If we have an average line length that is too high There's probably something wrong with this file Or it's probably auto generated But since we had almost 100 programming languages We should not use the same threshold For all the languages for this filt Because some programming languages just Have longer lines It's important to do some inspection And look at some samples from these languages

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: In our case, we had the BigCode community Which helps us look at 100 samples per extension And derive the appropriate thresholds and filtering Heuristics The third deduplicate sorry, filtering step Was neardeduplication We found that neardeduplication was the filtering that gave us The most performance boost It's also very easy to apply because it's language agnostic Even though we have 86 programming languages We don't need to change the duplication for each language We can just apply it to the whole sub To the whole data set And here I show you some results of the effects Of the duplication For example, here you can see this model Python all licensed If the filtering is done, you get a pass At one, which is our code metric of 13 But if you apply no duplication, you go from 13 to 17 That's a very big performance bump The same goes for other subsets permissive license We decided to use deduplication for our data set And to use strong deduplication to really remove

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: All the files that could be similar Another step is in our pipeline is To remove personal identifiable information This could be names, emails, or keys, or passwords Because we scraped code from GitHub And although GitHub has some tools To detect secrets and prompt users to remove them That's not always the case And we found that there was still A lot of secrets in the data sets And we train a model, you don't want It to be trained on that because in inference, it might generate Sensitive or personal data Our approach to removing it was to first annotate the data Sets for PII We collaborated with an annotation company To annotate some samples The annotators were tasked with the labeling PII When they found it For example, if they find the name, they give it a class name If you find an email, they also label it as an email It was a named entity recognition task And then we trained the StarPII, which Is our NER model to detect this PII

chunk_text: And then we run it on the whole StarCoder training data This took almost 800 GPU hours because it's a more It's a neural network and it needs to run on GPUs The last step in our filtering was data decontamination Because you should make sure to remove the benchmarks and test Sets from your training data Otherwise, your evaluation numbers will just be inflated We made sure to remove the benchmarks That we use for evaluation from our training sets The last step in the data curation of the stack Was to format the data Now that the data is filtered and because code Is different from text, we can allow Ourselves to apply some nice formatting that Could help us during inference For example, for StarCoder, we had the code file But before the code, we added some tokens That indicate that this is the repository name And another token file name that indicates the file Name and another one for stars And this is interesting because this model resembles StarCod

And see if the model would generate higher quality Code than if it were to generate for zero stars We didn't find any differences really during inference But it was fun to add all this formatting For StarCoder2, one of the improvements Was that StarCoder2 was repository aware Because when we have GitHub repositories, it's repository We have some files that are in the same repository that

chunk_text: Are related to each other But when we built the stack V1, we just Shuffled files so we kept we didn't Keep this repository structure And we trained the model, we just shuffled them And the model did not know if two files belong To the same repository But when we did StarCoder2, we try To keep files that are in the same repository Next to each other And how we did that is by concatenating them With some special tokens file SEP, which Separates files And this way, the model can know which Files need the same repository and try To find links between them 3D parallelism, and then you have also LightEval for doing The evaluation This is a stack to be able to run your full trainings But also your ablation models You can apply a filter from datatrove And then train with nanotron and evaluate with LightEval And they're well integrated togeth And they make one ecosystem That's for general LLMs For code LLMs, we also released the code

chunk_text: We used for both the stack and StarCoder models And our BigCode repository on GitHub And we just answered our third question, which Was how to filter the data Now, how to first, how much data you need And then where you can get this data, both web, and code And synthetic, and curated And you also know how you can properly filter the data And you can test the filtering techniques That you have in mind Now, let me tell you a little bit more about code LLMs Because that's what I'm working on And I'm trying to give you a little bit of an overview About these models so that how to train good LLMs But you also know how to build very cool code assistants And completion models How all of this started was when GitHub Copilot was released And it was very interesting because it was so much bett Than all the other code completion models that Were before it, which were very small and much less performance

chunk_text: And GitHub Copilot was using the Codex model by OpenAI And they just showed that you can train or code LLM In the same way that you train an for English, for example You can just take a large transformer model And give it a lot of code data and it will learn this code Because before, a lot of people were Trying to treat code very differently, for example By using abstract syntax trees But what Codex model showed is that you Can treat code text And if you want to predict the next line You can predict the next text, you just Do next token prediction and you get your code It works very well, much better compared to the more feature Engineering techniques And that was over two years ago and we didn't Have any good open code models But today, if you go to the hub, you can find that we have ov 1,700 models that are trained on code These are models that are either trained only

chunk_text: On code or LLMs that included code as part of their training You can see that we've made a lot of progress In this code generation field, which is amazing And this is the word this is the result of the committee's Work to build very good instructiontuned models And base models For example, here, as you can see in the leaderboard We have some very strong models that score almost 80 On the code evaluation benchmark, which Is human eval, which means they get almost 80 Of the problems right, which is a very large number And when talking about the landscape of open code LLMs In BigCode, we have released the stack data set Which is now the default data set for training On code, and also StarCoder1 and StarCoder2 two family of models And other instructiontuned models with the H2 team StarChat2 Meta also released some very good code models which are The code Llama series of models that go from 7B to 70B There are also the deep C models which are also very strong

chunk_text: And they have also other models the recent Granite models From IBM, CodeQwen, CodeGen, and StableCode There are different providers for code LLMs And also for data sets for code And the main reason we started the BigCode collaboration And to train our models was to have a collaboration where We have full data transparency We released all the details about the training But also the data is public so that people Can inspect it and use it And we also have the code for the processing and the model Weights And the collaboration was open We had over 1,000 researchers join our Slack and following The journey with us And this created a BigCode ecosystem Where the stack was used in the pretraining Of a lot of prominent code models CodeGen and StableCode And the StarCoder models were used As basis for a lot of community fine tuning And it's very important to be Aware of what makes a release of an LLM Whether it be a code LLM or general LLM

title: Stanford CS25: V4 I Behind the Scenes of LLM Pre-training: StarCoder Use Case
chunk_text: Open and responsible And this is fourfold First, it's really good for the community And for research in AI in general If you can make open access data sets, this will help This will mean having data inspection tools But also opt out tools to respect people's wishes Regarding their data sets For example, if they don't want to be included in the trainings They should be able to opt out It's also important to remove personal identifiable Information An open release does not mean just releasing model weights And stopping there, but also making your work reproducible By fully documenting the pipeline for using these models And also releasing tools for evaluation and technical reports That documents the whole pipeline And for us in BigCode, we went from SantaCoder Which was part of our ablations to understand how To filter the stack data sets And then we went to StarCoder which was released last year A 15 billion code generation model And then this year, we released StarCoder2

chunk_text: Which was trained on much more programming languages And had a much higher evaluation score And StarCoder was also rated as the most transparent model By the Stanford Foundation model transparency Index, which is really heartwarming given The efforts that we put into data governance And into making the model release as Transparent as possible Regarding evaluation, so for example, StarCoder 15B When it was released, it was the state of the art code model And this was also the case for StarCoder 215B among other 15B Models And it was even close or better than larger models I don't have the plot here, but it was better than It was matching code Llama 34B, and it was close to DeepSeek 33B On some benchmarks And here, for example, you can see the results On different benchmarks because when releasing our model It's really important that you don't just Evaluate on one benchmark, but you should add As many benchmarks as you want In case you had contamination, although we

chunk_text: Try to avoid this one benchmark, there's a very low chance That you also have contamination on other benchmarks And it also allows you to fully understand How your model behaves if you add more evaluation benchmarks And that's just a good practice that everyone should Be doing with their releases With the StarCoder models, we also released some tooling VS Code implementation, which also has a membership Test that tries to see if the generated code was In the training data and highlight that to the author That's part of our code attribution Efforts for these code models Maybe you're interested in using these models to build Your own personal Copilot and fine tuning StarCoder or Code Llama or other models on your personal code Bases To do that, there's a very nice blog post by Sourab and Sayak Where they try to take a code model And train it on the Hugging Face internal libraries And then deploy it in old Llama and have a local code assistant And the pipeline is very similar to what we did in pretraining

chunk_text: First, you take your data set, you Try to filter out the things you don't want to keep And then you do deduplication, and you train your model In this case, it will be just a fine tuning It will be much quicker You can use libraries PEFT which Do parameter efficient fine tuning where you don't need To train all the parameters of your models But you only inject few trainable parameters This makes the training much faster For example, 7B model can be trained in a Google Colab Now, let's go back to evaluation For example, for LLMs, there's The open LLM leaderboard that evaluates models There's also the LLMs arena, which compares instructs models And uses human evaluation For code models, one of the most popular benchmarks Is human eval And it's a benchmark where You have a function that the model has to autocomplete And then when the function is completed You take this solution and then you run it against multiple unit Tests and you count how many solutions pass

chunk_text: And how many solutions fail And then you count what we a metric that we call pass at one For example, this is the one that's Been reported in this leaderboard And this gives you the human eval score There's also a translation of this benchmark To 18 other languages Here, I show Java and JavaScript and C plus And this benchmark is called MultiPLE It allows you to see how well each model does On which programming language and choose the one that's The most interesting for you But these benchmarks usually have an issue Of contamination and overfitting, especially Instructiontuned models I don't know if you've already checked what these data sets Look , but usually for code, they Are an instruction that asks the model to generate an exercise And often, if you look at them, they Look really similar to human eval which Is function implementations There's a very high chance of having contamination Which means having some files that Look human eval exercises in your instruction tuning data

chunk_text: Here, for example, this plot is from the LiveCodeBench Leaderboard, and they find that some benchmarks may Be overfitting on human eval And so their solution was to have a leaderboard called LiveCodeBench where they regularly scrape New problems from platforms code contests and leaked code And they evaluate the models only On the problems that were released after the model release Date This way, they are sure that there is no contamination And for example, that was the case here They tried to evaluate these models on all the data they Have, and then they can compare the performance To the data that was only released after the model Release And they found that some models were not Consistent in their results That's one interesting thing to keep in mind And this is also another leader for this Will be interesting to compare not just open models, but also Closed models GPT4 and see where the open source Community is standing compared to these code models That was my presentation Thank you very much for your attention

chunk_text: And if you have any questions, I can answer them Yes, thank you very much for the great insightful talk We have some questions here on Slido I'm not sure if there are any inperson questions or else I will get started with the Slido question Sure Guess not I'll ask some of the questions online I had submitted some of these as well It seems there's some questions about synthetic data Let me see I was also wondering about this Someone's asking what are the consequences Of training AI models on AIgenerated synthetic data Do you foresee any problems with this And there's a related question Does synthetic data closely represent The natural distribution of language I assume some low quality data from humans Is necessary for things learning robustness And so forth Sure These are very great questions About the consequences of training models On AIgenerated data, I can think of two main ones First is enforcing some biases because models already Have some biases And if we train on data that is generated by them

chunk_text: Typical RLHF averages everything together What the authors do is they introduce a latent Variable for every user preference profile For example, a different demographic Children, adults, and so forth And trains reward models conditioned on these latent Vectors or factors This leads to something they call pluralistic alignment Which is improving the reward accuracy For these particular demographics or subgroups It enables a single model to adapt its behavior To different preference profiles and different demographics Or groups of people And now, I'll hand it back to Chelsea To talk about selfimproving All right Let's talk a little bit about selfimproving AI agents What exactly is an AI agent It's essentially a system that perceives the environment Makes decisions and takes actions towards achieving Some specific goal And usually, this goal is given by the human so for instance Gameplaying, tasksolving, or research assistance And there are several components of an AI agent One, it's goaldirected Two, it can make its own decisions Three, it can act iteratively Four, there's usually some memory component to it

chunk_text: And state tracking component to it And finally, there's some agents that Can use some tools such as API calls or function calling And finally, it can learn and adapt on its own Selfimprovement, , models Can reflect on their own outputs leading to iterative Improvements over time This typically consists of several steps There's some reflection of its own internal states There's an explanation of its own reasoning process It can evaluate the quality of its own outputs And finally, it can also simulate multistep reasoning Chains One technique is refinement This is where you have some iterative prompting technique Where an LLM critiques and improves its own outputs It generates some initial response And then refines it over time And this uses feedback loops to enhance the overall performance An example would be it generates some answ And then it evaluates itself for weaknesses and inconsistencies And finally, it refines the response Based on the own selfcritique method

title: Stanford CS25: V5 I Overview of Transformers
chunk_text: Another technique is called selfreflection This is where a model learns from past mistakes And adjusts future responses based on past failures There usually is some longterm memory component To this And an example would be the model first detects Some of weak response from its own outputs And then it reflects on its own mistakes And generates some improved answer to it And over multiple iterations, accuracy and reasoning Should improve over time Another technique is called ReAct, which is essentially Just combining reasoning with external actions such as API Calls or retrievals from a database And this is some model that can interact dynamically With its environment It gets feedback from taking multiple action sequences And incorporating that into its outputs For instance, the model will generate a reasoning plan And then it will call some external tool such as web search Or some API call, and then this model Incorporates the retrieved data into its final response

chunk_text: And finally, this leads us to a framework called Language Agent Tree Search What LATS is is that it Extends the ReAct framework to incorporate multiple planning Pathways You can think this analogous to chainofthought Versus treeofthought It gathers feedback from every path To improve the future search process, which Is some verbal reinforcement learninginspired technique And it uses Monte Carlo Tree Search To optimize planning trajectories Where in the tree structure, every node represents a state And every edge represents an action that the agent can take An example would be it generates N best new action Sequences, and then it will just execute them all in parallel Then it will use some selfreflection technique To score each one, and then overall Just continue exploring from the best state And update the probabilities of the past node

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: CHRISTOPHER POTTS Hello, everyone Welcome to part 6 in our series on supervised sentiment Analysis This screencast is going to cover two important methods In this space, hyperparameter search and classifi Comparisons Let's begin with hyperparameter search And first, I'll just offer the rationale Let's say that the parameters of a model Are those whose values are learned as part Of optimizing the model itself For the classifiers we've been studying The parameters are really just the weights That you learn on each of the individual features And those are the things that are directly targeted By the optimization process The parameters of a model are typically pretty Crisply defined because they follow From the structure mathematically of the model Under investigation Much more diffuse are the hyperparameters We can say the hyperparameters of a model Are any settings that are outside of the optimization Process mentioned in 1 Examples from models we've seen, our GloVe and LSA Have that dimensionality setting The model itself gives you no guidance About what to choose for the dimensionality

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: And the dimensionality is not selected As part of the optimization of the model itself You have to choose it via some external mechanism Making it a hyperparameter And GloVe has two other additional prominent Hyperparameters, xmax and alpha Again, those are not optimized by the model You have to select them via some external mechanism And for the classifiers that we've been studying We have regularization terms Those are classic hyperparameters If you have a deep classifier, then The hidden dimensionalities in the model Could also be considered hyperparameters Learning rates, any core feature of the optimization method Itself could be considered hyperparameters And even things that might be considered Architectural, the activation Function and the deep classifier You might think of it as an intrinsic part of the model That you're evaluating But since it's an easy choice point for us at this point You'll be tempted to explore a few different options For that particular architectural choice And in that way, it could become a hyperparameter And at this point, even the optimization methods

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Could also emerge as a hyperparamet That you would to do search over And so forth and so on, you should probably Take a fairly expansive view of what the hyperparameters Of your model are if you can Now here's the crux of the argument Hyperparameter optimization is crucial to building A persuasive argument Fundamentally, for any comparison we make We want to put every model in its very best light We could take it for granted that for any sufficiently Complicated model there's some setting of its hyperparameters That's degenerate and would Make the model look very bad And so you certainly wouldn't want To do any comparisons against that really problematic set Of choices Rather, what we want to do is say Let's put all the models in their best light By choosing optimal hyperparameters for them To the best of our ability And then we can say that one model is better than the oth If it emerges victorious in that very rigorous setting And the final thing I'll say about this methodologically

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Is that, of course, all hyperparameter tuning Must be done only on train and development data You can consider that all fair game in terms Of using it however you want to choose The optimal hyperparameters But once that choice is set, it is fixed And those are the parameters that you use at test time And that is the fundamental evaluation That you would use for any model comparison And at no point should you be tuning these hyperparameters On the test data itself That would be completely illegitimate I hope we've made it really easy to do This hyperparameter search In the context of the work you're Doing for supervised sentiment analysis Here are some code snippets that show how that can happen In loading my libraries, I have a point To our sentiment data And here I have a fixed feature function, which is just A unigram feature function The change happens inside the model wrapper Whereas before, essentially, all we did Was set up a logistic regression model

chunk_text: And then call its fit method, here we set up that model But also established a grid of hyperparameters These are different choice points For this logistic regression model Whether or not I have a bias Term, the value of the regularization parameter And even the algorithm used for regularization Itself, L1 or L2 The model will explore the full grid of these options It's going to do fivefold cross validation, so test one Each five times on different splits of the data And in that very long search process It will find what it takes to be the best setting of all Of these hyperparameters, of all the combinations That can logically be set And that is the model that we finally return here, right Now you can see the value of having a wrapp Around these fit methods Because then I could do all of this extra work Without changing the interface to sst.experiment at all The experiments look just as they did in the previous mode It's just that they will take a lot longer because you

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Are running dozens and dozens of experiments As part of this exhaustive search of all The possible settings Part 2 is classifier comparison Once again, begin with the rationale Suppose you've assessed a baseline Model B And your favorite model M. And your chosen assessment metric Favors M. And this seems a little victory for you But you should still ask yourself, is M really better Right Now if the difference between B and M Is clearly of practical significance Then you might not need to do anything beyond presenting The numbers, right If each one of your classification decisions Corresponds to something really important in the world And your classifier makes thousands More good predictions than the other model That might be enough for the argument But even in that situation, you might Ask whether there's variation in how these two models B and M perform Did you just get lucky when you saw What looked a practical difference And with minor changes to the initialization or something You would see very different outcomes

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: If the answer is possibly yes, then you Might still want to do some classifier comparison Now there's this nice paper by Demsar 2006 That advises using the Wilcoxon signedrank test for situations In which you can afford to repeatedly assess Your two models B and M on different train test splits Right And we'll talk later in the term about the precise rationale For this But the idea is just that you would do a lot of experiments On slightly different views of your data And then average across them To get a sense for how the two models compare with each other In situations where you can't repeatedly assess B and M McNemar's test is a reasonable alternative It operates on the confusion matrices produced by the two Models, testing the null hypothesis that the two models Have the same error rate The reason you might opt for McNemar's test Is, for example, if you're doing a deep learning Experiment where all the models take a few weeks to optimize

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Then of course, you can't probably Afford to do dozens and dozens of experiments with each one You might be compelled to use McNemar's based on one Single run of the two models It's a much weaker argument because, of course Precisely the point is that we might see variation Across different runs And McNemar's is not really going To grapple with that in the way that the Wilcoxon Signedrank test will But this is arguably better than nothing in most situations You might default to McNemar's if the Wilcoxon Is too expensive And let me just show you how easy This can be in the context of our code base By way of illustration, what we're essentially going to do Is compare logistic regression and naive Bayes I encourage you, when you're doing these comparisons To have only one point of variation We're going to fix the data and we're Going to fix the feature function And compare only the model architectures You could separately say I'm going To have a single fixed model logistic regression

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: And explore a few different feature functions But I would advise against exploring two different feature Functions as combined with two different models Because when you observe differences in the end You won't be sure whether that was caused by the model choice Or by the feature functions We want to isolate these things and do systematic comparisons Here, I'm going to do a systematic comparison Of logistic regression and naive Bayes On the SST using the Wilcoxon test And here's the setup The function is sstcomparemodels I point it to my training data You can have two feature functions But in that case, you should have just one model wrapper Here, I've got one feature function used for both models And I'll have these two different wrappers Corresponding to the evaluation that I Want to do of those two model classes I'm going to use the Wilcoxon as advised I'll do 10 trials of each on the train size of 70 of the data And as always, in this setting, I'll

title: Hyperparameter Search | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021

chunk_text: We're thinking about the task in the present day If you would additional perspectives On this, including some disputes about exactly how to think About the problem, and what would be the most productive I would encourage you to check out of these three papers By a lot of Stanford researchers The fundamental outcome of this Is that we do want to focus on common sense reasoning Even though that's a amorphous And difficult to define concept It's nonetheless arguably the useful one for us When we think about developing practical systems Now, in a visionary paper that really set the agenda For NLI, Dagan et al, 2006, they make A lot of connections between NLI and the broad Landscape of NLU Let me just read this opening statement here It seems that major inferences, as needed By multiple applications, can indeed Be cast in terms of textual entailment Consequently, we hypothesize that textual entailment Recognition is a suitable generic task For evaluating and comparing applied semantic inference Models Eventually, such efforts can promote the development

title: Adversarial Testing | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: CHRISTOPHER POTTS Welcome back, everyone This is part three in our series on NLI This is our chance to start getting a little introspective And think more about developing truly robust systems Our topic is going to be Dataset Artifacts And Adversarial Testing I'm pleased to report that a lot of the discussion in this area Traces, in the NLI context To a course project for this class In 2016, Leonid Keselman observed That for NLI, hypothesisonly models Were surprisingly strong What by hypothesisonly model Is that these are models that throw away The premise text, and reason entirely In terms of the hypothesis To the extent the models can succeed Despite having no information about the premise We might really worry about whether we're Solving the task we think we're solving Because after all NLI is supposed To be about the reasoning relationship between premise And hypothesis And you would not expect it to be successful if you Were given only the hypothesis But what Leonid observed, is that these models Were surprisingly strong

title: Adversarial Testing | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Subsequently, and partly independently A number of other groups made the same observation About a variety of NLI benchmarks And that leads us to the conclusion that at least For SNLI, averaging across a whole lot of different systems Hypothesisonly baselines are typically Operating in the range of about 65 to 70 accuracy Again, that's eye opening because chance performance Would be 33 And this is showing us that there Is some unusual bias in the hypothesis that Is allowing us to neglect the premise And still have a lot of predictive capacity The reason for this is likely due to what We're going to call artifacts in these datasets And just for a few examples here We can observe that specific claims Are likely to be premises in entailment cases And correspondingly general claims Are likely to be hypotheses in entailment cases Just think of the lexical level if you have A pair turtle and animal Where you have a very specific term in the premise And a very general term in the hypothesis

title: Adversarial Testing | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: That's an entailment relation, and if you Did just drop off the premise and looked only At the hypothesis animal you might still Have a pretty good guess that that's Going to be an entailment case in virtue Of the generality of the second term And relatedly specific claims are Likely to lead to contradiction The common strategy for creating a contradiction pair Is to just make sure you have two sentences that Exclude each other, in virtue of being very specific It's in virtue of patterns this, that a system denied The premise, can nonetheless succeed At about 65 to 70 accuracy Let's get a little more precise about what We mean by an artifact, because we need to think about this in a nuanced way My definition is that a dataset artifact Is a bias that would make a system Susceptible to adversarial attack Even if the bias is linguistically motivated And let me give you an example that Brings out the nuance there Consider negated hypotheses tending To signal contradiction

title: Adversarial Testing | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: This is a very natural thing linguistically If you give me a sentence the dog barked And you asked me to construct a contradictory sentence It's very natural for me to say the dog didn't bark By simply inserting a negation It's not a surprise that this happens It's linguistically motivated Negation is our best way of establishing the relevant connection However, here's the reason that this is an artifact We could easily curate a data set, in which negation Correlated with the other labels But nonetheless, this led to no human confusion Because humans are not really operating at this general level Of a dataset bias They are thinking about individual examples And what they mean But we know that our systems are going To be very sensitive to the distributions of things In their training data And that's the sense in which we can be adversarial in this way And expose that a system has overfit to a certain regularity Here are some known artifacts

title: Adversarial Testing | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: This is by no means exhaustive, but this will give you a sense for the things that you Want to look out for in an NLI context But also generally in dealing with problems in NLU It's been observed that these datasets contain Words whose appearance nearly perfectly Correlates with specific labels And what here is just randomly chosen words Cat and dog The reason for this is probably that crowd workers were Producing a lot of examples And they fell into a pattern of making Specific lexical choices And that created a spurious bias for one label or another Entailment hypotheses overrepresent General and approximating words We've seen that that's systematic in terms Of the linguistic patterns But it's an artifact because the world Needn't be this way for humans to succeed In making their predictions Neutral hypotheses often introduce modifiers This was a way that workers found To create statements that excluded each oth With simple modifications Contradiction hypotheses overrepresent negation We've seen that and that makes sense

title: Adversarial Testing | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: And neutral hypotheses tend to be longer And that last one is yet again another case Where that's the regularity That our systems are going to be very good at picking up on But that humans will probably not Make direct use of in making predictions of their own And in that way we can easily leverage this observation To create an adversarial setting for one of our models Where humans succeed at the task but our models suffer Because they're cued into the wrong aspects of the underlying Problem To close this out, I just want to emphasize That artifacts are discussed a lot in the context of NLI That's because a bunch of big benchmarks appeared And people did a lot of probing work to understand them But it does not follow that NLI is the only task where The datasets have artifacts In fact, I would venture that every task that we work on Has associated datasets that suffer from artifacts Here, I've given you a sample from prominent NLU problems

title: Adversarial Testing | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Where people have found artifacts That are similar to the ones that I just covered for NLI And the overall lesson is clear, whatever problem You're working on, you should think critically About your data, and how idiosyncrasies in that data Might be affecting system performance And creating a distance between what you think you're Doing, in terms of problem solving And what your system is doing And one way we can expose this is via efforts Involving adversarial testing We're going to have a whole discussion of this Later in the quarter But I do want to plant the idea here In adversarial testing we're going To take standard NLI examples this And modify them in ways that expose that systems Have surprising gaps A prominent early example of this Is this wonderful paper by Glockner et al Called Breaking NLI What they did is very simple, we're Going to operate with actual SNLI examples Here we would start with the premise A little girl is kneeling in the dirt crying

title: Adversarial Testing | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021

chunk_text: CHRISTOPHER POTTS Welcome, everyone This is part 5 in our series on natural language inference We're going to be talking about attention mechanisms Attention was an important source of innovation in the NLI Literature, and, of course, it's only Grown in prominence since then Let's begin with some guiding ideas In the context of the NLI problem We might have an intuition that we just need more connections For a lot of our architectures between the premise And hypothesis, right Possibly, in processing the hypothesis We just need the model to have some reminders about what The premise contained And whatever summary representation we have Of that premise might just not be Enough from the point of view of processing the hypothesis And feeding the representation into the classifier layer Relatedly, there's a persistent intuition in the NLI literature That it's useful to softly align the premise and the hypothesis To find corresponding words and phrases between those two Texts It can be difficult to do that at a mechanical level

title: Attention | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: But attention mechanisms might allow Us, via our datadriven learning process To find soft connections in the weights for these attention Layers between the premise and hypothesis And achieve some of the effects that we would get From a real alignment process Let's begin with global attention This is the simplest attention mechanism That you see in the NLI literature But it's already quite powerful And as you'll see, it has deep connections with the attention Mechanisms in the transformer To make this concrete, let's start with a simple example We have every dog danced as our premise Some poodle danced as our hypothesis And they're fit together into this chained RNN model for NLI Now, standardly, what we would do Is take this final representation, hC As the summary representation for the entire sequence And feed that directly into the classifier What we're going to do when we add attention mechanisms is Instead offer some connections back from this state Into the premise states The way that process gets started Is via a series of dot products

title: Attention | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: We're going to take our target vector HC, and take its dot product with each one Of the hidden representations corresponding to tokens In the premise And that gives us this vector of unnormalized scores Just the dot products And it's common, then, to softmax Normalize those scores into our attention weights, alpha What we do with alpha is then create our context vector And the way that happens is that we're Going to get a weighted view of all those premise states Each one h1, h2, and h3 Is weighted by its corresponding attention weight, which Is capturing its unnormalized notion Of similarity with our target vector hC And then to get a fixed dimensional version of that We take the mean or it could be the sum Of all of those weighted views of the premise Next, we get our attention combination layer And there are various ways to do this One simple one would be to simply concatenate our context Vector with our original context Target vector hC and feed those through a dense lay

title: Attention | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Of learned parameters Another perspective, similar Is to give the context vector and our target vector HC, each one their own weights, and have An additive combination of those two And, again, feed it through some nonlinearity And you could think of various other designs for this And that gives us this attention combination, h tilde And then, finally, the classifier lay Is a simple dense layer, just as before, except instead Of using just hC, we now use this h tilde representation Which incorporates both hC and that weighted mixture Of premise states It might be useful to go through this With some specific numerical values here What I've done is, just imagine That we have twodimensional representations for all Of these vectors And you can see, what I've done here is ensure that Proportionally, every is a lot this final representation Here And then that similarity drops off As we move through the premise states And you'll see what happens when we take the dot products here The first step gives us the unnormalized scores

chunk_text: Is proportional to that unnormalized similarity There are other scoring functions that you could use Of course We've just done a simple dot product up here But you can also imagine having learned parameters in there Or doing concatenation of the learned parameters This does a bilinear form And this is just a concatenation of those two states fed Through these learned weights And once you see this design space You can imagine there are a lot of other ways In which you could mix in parameters And have different views of this global attention mechanism We could go one step further here That was global attention In wordbyword attention, we're going To have a lot more learned parameters and a lot More connections between the hypothesis back Into the premise To make this tractable I've picked one pretty simple view of how this could work And the way we should track these computations Is focus on this vector B here, because we're Going to move through time But let's imagine that we've already processed the A state

chunk_text: Welcome, everyone, to the first screencast In our NLU and information retrieval series The goal of this introductory screencast is twofold I will first introduce the IR area Then I will discuss ways in which NLU and IR can Interact productively and focus on how retrieval Can be an effective component in defining our NLU tasks And building our NLU systems What is information retrieval or IR To a first approximation, this is the field Concerned with search The first example that typically comes to mind is web search But as we'll see today, this field Extends richly beyond web search and has strong connections To our work with NLU Let's now attempt to define IR more formally Here is a simplified version of the definition Used by the Introduction to IR book by Manning et al They define IR as the process of finding material that fulfills An information need from within a large collection Of unstructured documents Let's unpack this definition Starting on the lefthand side here The definition says that we're concerned with finding material

title: NLU and Information Retrieval | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: From a large collection In other words, large scale search is at the essence of IR On the righthand side, the definition Restricts this to unstructured documents, items Text, media, and products, ones That lack the clear cut structure of things Database tables or graphs Structurebased search or structurebased traversal Of graphs and databases are not typically considered IR problems for our purposes, although, of course They're interesting on their own right This leads us to the term that was At the center of our definition, namely the information need It is difficult to think of IR without thinking Of the user at the center of the system And the information need is what the user has in Mind to solve a task or otherwise learn or reach The material that they are looking for The goal of a search system is first to identify and fulfill The user's information need Whatever we retrieve is only going To be considered relevant to the extent That it advances this goal In most IR tasks, the user would explicitly

title: NLU and Information Retrieval | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Provide us with a query that summarizes and expresses Their information need It is very important to note that this query may contain Ambiguity, may miss some important details Or might even sometimes ask the wrong question And that's completely normal The user may not even be sure what precisely they're Looking for That's why they're searching for something And so, we must rely on our knowledge of the task And whatever we know about the user within the constraints Of our application in order to solve IR problems The second thing is that typical information needs vary by task And so the typical information need that we have And how to best interpret and deal with that These are factors that vary greatly By task and by collection type in IR I'll take it you've already made the connection between IR And searching the web, searching your email And also finding files in your desktop buried in deep folders Or something But there are plenty of other IR tasks where search is crucial

title: NLU and Information Retrieval | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: For instance, you might want to find Recent papers related to the BERT paper by Devlin et al Of course, this is not the best example Because there are many, many papers related To BERT these days But in any case, in this case, your query Might be the full text of the BERT paper And the system might try to search the ACL Anthology and the computational language Section of archives for some of their papers to BERT Recommendation is another key IR topic In recommendation, we still seek relevant material From a large collection of unstructured items But, in this case, the user has no explicit query And instead, the previous interactions Enabled the recommendation system to suggest the matches Patent search is yet another IR task And unlike the others we've mentioned so far It's often used by experts, not by average users And it has very strong emphasis on hierarchy Unlike the average web query where You might be completely content with one very good match At the top, patent search may need

title: NLU and Information Retrieval | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: To find every relevant patent to a query or something that Approximates that Lastly, even buying a new laptop can be an IR problem And in particular, a conversation of an IR problem Here, the system may go in a back and forth style Between searching for relevant products And asking the user for their preferences about cost, screen Quality, and storage, and other factors On online ecommerce platforms Having looked at all of these IR tasks It's important to keep in mind that each of those tasks Poses its own unique challenges Even though we're always interested in relevance And in finding relevant items, each of those tasks Has its own challenges and its own components To underscore this, let's use web search As a frame of reference While standard web search might pose considerable challenge When it comes to the massive scale involved in terms Of documents and also queries, even something As seemingly mundane as searching for conversations On your Slack workspace often lacks Key features that makes web search

title: NLU and Information Retrieval | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Tractable in the first place and makes It work the way it does in the first place For one, so many web searches ask frequently searched or head Queries The sheer popularity of head queries Makes them an easy target for large search engines Of course, there's always a long tail of various search queries That still pose considerable challenge, especially In highly technical domains, but it still Stands that, in a domain web search Solving the head queries gets you a very big part A very big share of answering most user queries There's another factor Web search enjoys highly redundant documents Out there that address common topics Where each document is written in a slightly different way This often shifts the search problem into a precision one Finding some documents, at least One, that definitely match the query, as opposed To a recall one Finding every document that matches the query Because there's already too many of them Clearly, this is not always the case If you're looking for a very specific item in your Slack

chunk_text: Conversation and history Yet another factor in web search is the rich link structure That links between existing related web pages, which Again introduces more hierarchy and might make this task more Tractable in practice The idea here is definitely not that web search is easy Because it's not easy But the different tasks pose different challenges For our IR systems That is IR Where does our work on NLU fit in IR Of course, queries and documents Are often expressed in natural language, a decent part We naturally want to understand a query's meaning And its intent and understand the document's contents And their topics to be able to effectively match queries To documents This form of understanding is critical Although you can go pretty far for many IR tasks With intelligently matching terms at a lexical level The vocabulary mismatch problem makes this quite unattractive In practice To explain, vocabulary mismatch happens When queries and documents use different terms To refer to the same thing I have here on the slide an example query

chunk_text: Onto our more central question, where does IR Fit into our study of NLU, and how can IR serve us In thinking about this, I believe It's helpful to appreciate that as our models become More advanced in NLU, they too, humans, start To have complete information needs in solving their tasks More concretely, retrieval can contribute to our NLU tasks And systems in three exciting ways First, retrieval provides a rich source For creating challenging and realistic NLU tasks, ones Where finding information from a large corpus is essential We will look closely at this bullet in the remaind Of these slides Second, retrieval offers a powerful tool To make NLU models for existing tasks more accurate and more Effective We'll touch upon this today, but we'll discuss it in more depth Later Third, retrieval can often lend us A nice framework for evaluating NLU systems whenever the output Domain is large, just in search Or whenever low latency is important Which are key characteristics in IR

chunk_text: Of improving quality and coverage Just take a model, train a larger version of it On more data and hope that that includes more knowledge And gives you more accurate results As an alternative to this, you could Think about open book approaches to opendomain question Answering There's the analogy of doing an open book exam, which Tests not really your memory but your awareness of where To look for answers and how to use them quickly And productively In this case, we will build what are typically Called retrieveandread architectures As shown at the bottom of the slide, we take the question And first feed it to a retrieval model The retriever searches our collection of facts In this case, Wikipedia as an example And extracts a bunch of passages or other contexts That seem useful in trying to answer the original question These passages are then fed to a downstream reader That could just be a small BERT model Which studies these passages to answer the original question

chunk_text: OMAR KHATTAB Hello, everyone Welcome to part 2 of our series on NLU and IR The screen cast will be a crash course in classical IR As well as evaluation methods and information retrieval Let us first define the simplest form of our task Namely ranked retrieval We will be given a large collection of text documents This could be all of the passages in Wikipedia Perhaps a crawl of parts of the web Or maybe all of the documentation of Hugging Face Or other software libraries This corpus will be provided to us offline, that is before we Interact with any users And we will be able to spend a one time effort at organizing Or otherwise understanding the content Of these documents in the corpus before we start searching Online though, we will receive a query From the users, which could be a natural language Question written in English, for example The goal of our ranked retrieval system Will be to output a TopK list of documents, sorted

chunk_text: In decreasing order of relevance to the information Need that the user expressed in the query This might be the top 10 or the top 100 results How do we conduct this task of ranked retrieval As it turns out, we've already looked at the way For doing this before, when discussing matrix designs In particular, we know that we can build TermDocument Occurrence Matrices And in such a matrix the one shown Each termdocument pair has a corresponding cell In which the matrix will store the number of times That the term appears in the document, in our corpus Of course, we will probably want to apply Some reweighting here, because we don't want To work with these row counts But once we've done that, we can already Answer queries that contain just a single term pretty well And to do that, we would just return The Kdocuments with the largest weight After normalization or other processes for the single term And again, as it turns out, this is precisely what

title: Classical IR | Stanford CS224U Natural Language Understanding | Spring 2021
chunk_text: Is done in classical IR if we have just a single query Just a single term in our query When we have multiple terms in the same query Classical IR tends to treat them independently We would add the weights up Across all of the terms in the query per document And then, that's the score for the document This is precisely the computation That is shown here, where we compute the relevance score Between a query and a document We would go over all the terms in the query And simply add the corresponding documentterm weights For all of these terms for that document This gives us a score for the document And we can then return the Kdocuments With the largest total scores Interestingly, this reduces much of classical IR Of course, not all of it, to thinking About how do we best weigh each termdocument pair, which Has an undeniable similarity to our first task This quarter in Homework 1 Except of course, that here in IR We look at the term to document relevance, and not word
